First, we isolate the exponential term:

$$
\begin{aligned}2\cdot {6}^{x+1}+4 & <1 \\ 2\cdot {6}^{x+1} & <-3 \\ {6}^{x+1} & <-\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, recall that a positive number raised to any real power is always positive. Since $6>0,$ we have

$$
{6}^{x+1}>0
$$

for every real value of $x.$

Therefore, ${6}^{x+1}$ cannot be less than $-\frac{3}{2}.$ Hence, the inequality

$$
{6}^{x+1}<-\frac{3}{2}
$$

has no solutions.

First, we find the principal value:

$$
\begin{aligned}x=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(-\frac{1}{4})=-0.252\,680…≈-0.252\,7\end{aligned}
$$

Since $-0.252\,7$ lies inside the given domain, our first solution is ${x}_{1}=-0.252\,7.$

Our first solution lies in the fourth quadrant and has a reference angle of ${\theta }_{R}=0.252\,7.$ Since $\operatorname{sin}⁡x<0,$ the second solution must lie in the third quadrant, and it also has a reference angle ${\theta }_{R}=0.252\,7.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14066983/assets/8cb3c3ad525f606ec5cc6ef3961577666ab7117b3ce2a17014df989dcb105f57.png)

A second solution $X$ lies in the $3$rd quadrant, and we can find it using the reference angle as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}X & =\pi +{\theta }_{R} \\  & =\pi +0.252\,7 \\  & ≈3.394\,3\end{aligned}
$$

However, this value is not in the required domain. To get the second solution ${x}_{2}$ that's within the given domain, we simply subtract $2\pi :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2}=X-2\pi  & =3.394\,3-2\pi ≈-2.888\,9\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally,

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}=(-0.252\,7)\cdot (-2.888\,9)≈0.7,
$$

rounded to $1$ decimal place.

Recall that when a particle moves with constant acceleration, the velocity vector at time $t$ can be found using

$$
v=u+at,
$$

where $u$ is the initial velocity, and $a$ is the acceleration of the particle.

Here, we have

$$
u=6i-2j,\,a=-i+4j.
$$

Therefore, after $t=3\,\text{h},$ the velocity of the particle will be

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =u+at \\  & =(6i-2j)+(-i+4j)(3) \\  & =(6i-2j)+(-3i+12j) \\  & =(3\,i+10\,j)\,\text{km/h}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the speed of the particle is

$$
\begin{aligned}|v| & =|3i+10j| \\  & =\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{10}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9+100} \\  & =\sqrt{109}\,\text{km/h}.\end{aligned}
$$
